vignette:
# Marcus

Marcus is a 29-year-old Coast Guard officer who works in search and rescue operations along the northeastern coast. He's been with his partner, David, for three years, and they live together in a modest house near the station. By all accounts, Marcus was a dedicated, level-headed professional—the kind of person colleagues trusted in high-pressure situations. That was before the night everything changed.

Fourteen months ago, Marcus was walking home from a late shift around midnight. He'd taken this route hundreds of times, cutting through a quieter neighborhood to save time. He remembers it was cold, the streets mostly empty. A man approached from behind, and before Marcus could fully process what was happening, he was shoved against a brick wall. There was a knife—Marcus can still see the blade in his peripheral vision, though he's never entirely certain it was real or if his mind has reconstructed it that way. The attacker demanded his wallet, his phone, his watch. Marcus gave everything. The whole thing lasted maybe two minutes, but those minutes fractured something fundamental in how he experiences the world.

The physical injuries healed quickly—bruises on his ribs and shoulder, a cut on his hand from trying to protect himself. But Marcus hasn't healed in the ways that matter. He's become someone he doesn't recognize.

At work, Marcus struggles through his shifts in a state of constant vigilance. During rescue operations, his mind splits between the task at hand and an exhausting internal alarm system. He finds himself scanning faces of rescued individuals, checking their hands, their pockets, assessing threats that aren't there. His supervisor has noticed he's become overly cautious, sometimes hesitant in situations where quick decisions are necessary. Last month, during a routine training exercise, a colleague touched his shoulder unexpectedly and Marcus reacted so violently—spinning around, fists raised—that the room went silent. He was mortified, but he couldn't stop shaking for an hour afterward.

Sleep has become a battleground. Most nights, Marcus lies awake beside David, his body rigid, listening to every sound in the house. When he does sleep, he's back in that alley—sometimes the knife is larger, sometimes there are multiple attackers, sometimes it happens in his own home. He wakes gasping, drenched in sweat, and David's presence, which should be comforting, sometimes triggers panic instead. Marcus has begun sleeping in the guest room, telling himself it's because he doesn't want to disturb David, though the real reason is more complicated. Being touched while vulnerable terrifies him.

In public spaces, Marcus exists in a state of coiled tension. He positions himself with his back to walls in restaurants. He avoids crowds. A few weeks ago, he abandoned his shopping cart at the grocery store and left when a man in dark clothing stood near him. He knows it's irrational. He knows the man was just shopping. But knowing and feeling are different things.

David has tried to be patient, but the distance between them has grown palpable. Marcus can see the worry in his partner's eyes, the careful way David now asks before touching him. They haven't been intimate since the attack. Marcus wants to want that connection, but his body has become a stranger to him—hypersensitive and unreliable.

Marcus still goes to work. He still functions. But there's a hollowness to it now, a sense that he's going through the motions of his own life while watching from somewhere distant. He's begun to wonder if this version of himself—hypervigilant, isolated, trapped in a loop of fear and shame—is permanent.
